newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.K. forces mark last HK remembrance day before '97.
newsitem.headline: U.K. forces mark last HK remembrance day before '97.

text.p: Hong Kong's colonial government and the British garrison commemorated the war dead on Sunday on the territory's last Remembrance Day under British rule.

After the British anthem was played, Governor Chris Patten and Commander of the British Forces in Hong Kong, Major General Bryan Dutton, laid wreaths at a Cenotaph memoralizing servicemen who lost their lives for the colony in wars.
They were followed by respresentatives of war veterans and other parties from different sectors of the community, who laid a total of about 100 wreaths at the memorial.
More than 50 veterans from World War Two, including some who had flown from as far away as Britain, attended the ceremony.
The annual Remembrance Day commemorates the end of World War One on November 11, 1918. It is usually observed in Hong Kong on a Sunday as an occasion to remember the war dead in both wars.
Some British soldiers were sent from Hong Kong to fight in World War One although there was no fighting in the territory.
In World War Two, the Japanese invaded the colony from China, crossing the border on December 8, 1941, at about the same time as the attack on Pearl Harbour on the other side of the date line.
Hong Kong held out for more than two weeks despite overwhelming odds, defended by a tiny, lightly armed garrison aided by volunteers. It fell 17 days later on Christmas Day.
Thousands of British and Commonwealth prisoners of war were interned in camps in the territory. Others were transported to Japan and Taiwan to become vitual slave labourers.

Hong Kong reverts to China next July 1 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule. The British garrison will have pulled out by the handover, to be replaced by the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA).
There is concern whether the post-handover government will celebrate the Remembrance Day after the sovereignty transfer.
"I don't think this will carry on," said a 88-year-old ex-soldier who fought here in World War Two. "I hope I'm wrong."
But some have voiced their faith that China will give its blessing.
Veterans hope the annual commemoration will stay, and some have vowed to continue rememberances for their fallen comrades even if they have to move to a private venue.

"So many people fought in World War One and World War Two for so many years. So many of them died. They should be commemorated. It's not a question of nationality," said 79-year-old Leung Kwan, an ex-serviceman.
Patten said he expected the post-handover government to have some representation in next year's Remembrance Day celebration.
"That will be a matter for my successor but I think that it would be surprising if there was not some government representation," he said.

"After all, what we are remembering is those who sacrificed their lives, not least to defend Hong Kong and its freedoms, and those who sacrificed their lives included very many brave local Chinese," he said.

The arrival of China's PLA Army in Hong Kong next year is veiwed with some trepidation in the territory, as images of the the army's 1989 crackdown on student demcoracy protestors around Tiananmen Square in Beijing remains etched in Hong Kong's collective memory.

After the wreath-laying ceremony on Sunday, war veteran Jack Edwards staged a demonstration at the Cenotaph to urge for an early issuing of British passports to wives and widows of local servicemen who fought in World War Two.
"I am fighting for the wives and war widows who still haven't got their passports," he said.
British Prime Minister John Major promised them British passports during a visit in Hong Kong in March, after a marathon campaign led by Edwards.
